newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China, Taiwan, HK stocks mixed as Deng factor fades.
newsitem.headline: China, Taiwan, HK stocks mixed as Deng factor fades.

text.p: Stocks in China and Taiwan rose on Friday while those in Hong Kong fell as the focus began to shift back to fundamental factors and away from the death of China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping.
The markets had ended higher on Thursday once Deng's death, which occurred late on Wednesday, was perceived as removing a major element of uncertainty from the markets.
By Friday, Asian markets largely took a breather, particularly after an overnight sell-off on Wall Street, where the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 92 points to 6,927.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index was off 35.75 points, or 0.27 percent, at 13,375.58.
"There is a lot of two-way trading," said Anthony Mak, sales director at Vickers Ballas. "Some are taking profits but some are going back in (to buy)," he said.
Other traders noted that the reappointment on Thursday of Hong Kong's top civil servents to the post-colonial administration was being viewed positively by the market.
"Basically all these senior government officials remain unchanged so that is very important to maintain a stable transition," said Ben Kwong, director of research at Dharmala Securities.
Shares on the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges were higher on Friday on buying by both retail investors and institutions, brokers said.
"Both institutions and individuals...believe a major negative factor on the stock markets has been permanently removed with Deng's death confirmed," one China trader said.
Brokers said securities houses in Shanghai held meetings on Wednesday and agreed on the need to keep markets stable but not intervene to support them.
"Heads of the securities brokerages agreed that there was no need to intervene in the markets because they believed the markets would not plunge," said one executive with a Chinese brokerage.
Shanghai's foreign-currency B share index was up 0.666 points, or 1.03 percent, to 65.341, while domestic A shares were up 31.437 points, or 3.12 percent, to 1,039.168.
Shenzhen's B share index was up 3.97 points, or 2.76 percent at 147.50, while the A share index fluctuated in a narrow range and was up 2.45 points, or 0.7 percent, at 353.05.
Taiwan stocks rallied to a six-year high after the government late on Thursday announced gross domestic product for the fourth quarter of 1996 was 6.62 percent, above an expected 6.58 percent.
The weighted index shrugged off Deng's death to climb 113.15 points or 1.47 percent to end at 7,791.19. It was the highest close since June 2, 1990, when the index ended at 7,857.01.
Singapore stocks slipped, with the Straits Times Index down 14.66 points, or 0.65 percent, at 2,237.32.
Tokyo stocks were up modestly on scattered buying of property and bank stocks. The key Nikkei 225-share index was up 8.11 points, or 0.25 percent, at 19,099.82.
Philippine shares were off 8.45 points, or 0.26 percent, at 3,301.98, while Indonesian shares lost 0.756 points, or 0.11 percent, to 697.913.
Korean shares were off 11.62 points, or 1.63 percent, at 699.51. Concern over rising interest rates dampened sentiment.
Australian stocks lost 2.7 points, or 0.11 percent, to 2,473.6, while New Zealand shares were down 24.32 points, or 1.05 percent, at 2,301.53.

The dollar recovered slightly from overnight losses but the near-term direction was unclear. In Tokyo, the U.S. currency was quoted at around 123.01 yen, compared with 122.50 at the close in New York and at 1.6874 marks against 1.6863.
